current_episode.title: 127. NYC Investment Sales 1H 2026: Following the Capital, Not the Noise with Shimon Shkury

guest.bio_context: Shimon Shkury is a commercial real estate investment sales professional at Ariel Property Advisors with deep expertise in New York City's multifamily, office, and retail markets. He has transacted numerous high-value deals including project-based Section 8 affordable housing sales and office-to-residential conversion projects across Manhattan.

context.transcript_excerpt: Good morning and welcome to the Coffee and Cap Rates podcast, your go-to source for New York City's latest commercial real estate insights. This program is brought to you by Ariel Property Advisors. I'm going to start with a story because a few months ago, a friend who's also in real estate called me up and said, Shimon, what are you still doing in New York City? You should come to Miami. See, in Florida, they lack business. And you know what? He's not alone. When you listen to the noise, you might think that New York City doesn't have an opportunity anymore. But when you look at the numbers, something very different emerges. We've had about $17.4 billion of investment sales transactions in the first six months of 2026. That's a 37% increase year over year. So capital is here, but it's selective. What you're going to see throughout this presentation in each one of these asset classes is that capital is investing in reset valuations, in fundamentals that are growing, in policy alignments. And when all of those don't exist, capital is looking for distress and basis. I'm going to start with the multifamily asset class. And there, not only we had growth, we also have three specific groups. We have free market multifamily, affordable housing, and rent-stabilized multifamily assets. They each behave differently. I'm going to start with a free market multifamily, where most of the transactions take place. And there, investors are looking for yesterday's pricing with today's fundamentals. The values of free market buildings today, on average, are about 16% below what they were at peak, where rents have grown by 60%, almost 60%, in the past six years. That's a very compelling investment thesis for institutional investors. One of the transactions that took place earlier this year is the Columbus Square transaction. MetLife and UDR bought this deal in 2012, and MetLife sold their stake to Carmel Partners earlier this year for a 23% discount. It's the same asset, three different investors, three different decisions. Carmel Partner enters into a discounted deal. UDR stays for the upside potential and the accretive debt. Institutions weren't the only ones investing. It was about deregulated buildings and value-add, and smaller tax-class protected deals, where private and international investors invested. So when it comes to free market multifamily, we have a deep bench of investors. It's all about the recent valuations and the growing fundamentals. Affordable housing is very different. There it's all about the private-public alignment, and there are many different iterations and asset classes within affordable housing. One that is more aligned than others is project-based Section 8. There, the lower rents are complemented by rent subsidies, by property tax abatements, by the opportunity to lend from HUD and agency, and so the mission to provide quality housing for lower-income families is coupled with the ability of investors to get a return. Very few people know more about affordable housing than Robert Nelson, who manages and invests in thousands of units, and he's going to be one of our panelists soon. In the past six months, we've seen many project-based Section 8 transactions. Only three of them are here, two of which our company has sold for $120 million together. Project-based Section 8 also held its value compared to free market. Both of them got a recent valuation, but project-based Section 8 was closer to the free market world than to the rent-stabilized world, and that's meaningful, because it encourages investors to reinvest in it and preserve affordability. Where did we see misalignment? You guessed right, in rent-stabilized multifamily. There, we had rents that are low, with no ability to increase them through subsidies or tax abatements. pending_qa.q: Which office asset classes performed strongest in commercial real estate investment during the first half of 2026?
pending_qa.r: Class A office, Class B office being repositioned, and office-to-residential conversions were the three main performing categories. Class A office saw 23 million square feet leased in the past six months alone, primarily to high-end law firms, financial institutions, and tech companies, driven by the integrated experience combining office, hospitality, and quality-of-life amenities.

pending_qa.q: What is the current pipeline for office-to-residential conversion units in New York City?
pending_qa.r: Approximately 16,000 units are currently in the pipeline to be converted from office to residential over the past two years. One of 65 office-to-residential transactions that traded in this period was 101 Greenwich, illustrating the scale and momentum of this asset class transformation.

pending_qa.q: How do tax abatement programs like 467M incentivize office-to-residential conversions?
pending_qa.r: The 467M tax abatement program allows developers to make economic sense of office-to-residential conversions while allowing the city to receive 25% of the resulting units as affordable housing. This policy alignment between developer economics and public housing goals has generated significant transaction activity in this space.

pending_qa.q: What is the annual housing supply gap in New York City relative to production capacity?
pending_qa.r: The city needs to produce approximately 60,000 units per year to catch up to the lack of supply, but is currently producing only about half of that. When accounting for losses in rent-stabilized units, actual net production is approximately one-third of the needed supply.

pending_qa.q: How are retail property markets changing in terms of investor ownership patterns?
pending_qa.r: Brands are increasingly buying their own permanent retail locations rather than leasing; examples include VanCleef purchasing their own lease on Madison Avenue, joining Prada and Gucci from prior years. Additionally, retail service companies occupying physical space—businesses that cannot be purchased on Amazon—are driving continued demand for brick-and-mortar retail real estate.

pending_qa.q: What key market indicators should commercial real estate investors monitor going forward?
pending_qa.r: Investors should watch interest rates as a top priority, monitor changes in the economy and stock market that could affect property fundamentals, track mortgage maturities both as sources of distressed deals and refinancing activity at higher rates, and closely follow city policy decisions regarding preservation of affordable housing and rent-stabilized housing.
